annotation_description: Chose to be on the draw in Modern without Gemstone Caverns in hand. Being on the play is almost universally preferred in Modern, especially with a ramp/tempo strategy featuring Ugin's Labyrinth and Sowing Mycospawn that benefits from deploying threats a turn earlier.

message: Select a card (2 more) to put on the bottom of your library
annotation_description: Qwen3L Stoic is mulliganing and bottoming Emrakul, the Promised End, which is the key card to exile with Ugin's Labyrinth to generate 2 colorless mana per turn. The hand has Ugin's Labyrinth + Emrakul, which is one of the strongest openings possible - play Labyrinth turn 1 exiling Emrakul for 2 mana, then Talisman turn 2, enabling a turn 3 Icetill Explorer or Sowing Mycospawn. Without Emrakul, Ugin's Labyrinth only produces 1 colorless mana (no card with mana value 7+ to imprint), making it significantly worse. Sowing Mycospawn is colorless but only has mana value 4, which doesn't meet the 7+ requirement for imprint. Bottoming Emrakul destroys the hand's synergy.

message: Select a card (1 more) to put on the bottom of your library
annotation_description: Sowing Mycospawn is one of the deck's key payoff cards - it searches for a land when cast and can exile an opponent's land when kicked. With Ugin's Labyrinth in hand but no colorless card with mana value 7+ to imprint, the Labyrinth only produces {C}. However, Sowing Mycospawn is the only card in hand that could potentially be ramped into as a meaningful threat. The hand has two Talismans, two lands, and Icetill Explorer for ramp, making it well-suited to cast a 4-mana spell on turn 3. Bottoming the Mycospawn removes the primary payoff for all that ramp. Bottoming a second Talisman of Impulse would be more reasonable since having two is redundant - you likely only need one accelerant alongside the lands.

Qwen3L Stoic had two lands in play (a Forest from the fetched Verdant Catacombs) and could cast Talisman of Impulse for {2}. With a Forest producing {G} and presumably another land, they had the mana to deploy a Talisman, accelerating toward Icetill Explorer on turn 3. Instead they passed, losing a full turn of mana development. The reasoning incorrectly states they couldn't cast it, but Talisman costs {2} (generic mana) and they should have had access to 2 mana from their lands.

Casting a ritual during combat is wasteful because mana empties between phases. The RRR generated would drain away before main phase 2, effectively wasting the ritual card and gaining nothing. The player has no instants or abilities that could meaningfully use the mana during combat.

Casting Pyretic Ritual during combat with no meaningful way to use the RRR mana it produces. The mana pool empties at end of phase/step, and there's nothing productive to spend it on during combat. This wastes the card entirely. The player likely intended to ramp into something, but ritual mana needs to be used in the same step it's generated, and the player has no instants or abilities that would benefit from 3 red mana during combat.

With only 2 mana available (Gemstone Caverns + Sacred Foundry), the player cast Ruby Medallion for 2 mana, using their entire turn. However, Strike It Rich costs only R (1 mana) and creates a Treasure token, which would have given them 3 mana next turn (2 lands + Treasure) to cast Ruby Medallion AND still have mana left, or cast Wrenn's Resolve to dig for more resources. By casting Ruby Medallion first, they get no immediate value this turn and only have 3 mana sources next turn (2 lands + Medallion's discount). Casting Strike It Rich first would have been better sequencing - it generates a Treasure token for next turn, enabling a 3-mana turn where they could play Ruby Medallion and still have the Medallion discount available going forward, or play Wrenn's Resolve to find more action. The difference is small but Strike It Rich into Ruby Medallion next turn is slightly more efficient sequencing.

Declined to play a land on turn 4 with only 1 land (Shifting Woodland) on the battlefield. With 2 lands in hand (Ugin's Labyrinth and Verdant Catacombs), skipping this land drop leaves them hopelessly behind on mana development against an opponent who is already casting spells.

Casting Wish before Strike It Rich and before cracking Bloodstained Mire is suboptimal sequencing. Strike It Rich costs 0 with Ruby Medallion out, creating a Treasure token for free mana. The player should play land/crack fetch first and cast free spells before committing mana to Wish. Additionally, Wish fetches a card from outside the game (sideboard), which in many contexts may not provide meaningful value, and the mana spent on Wish (3 mana) could have been better sequenced with the cheaper spells first to maximize information and mana efficiency.

Qwen3L Stoic cast Talisman of Impulse using both available lands (Forest + Shifting Woodland) instead of playing Ugin's Labyrinth first. Ugin's Labyrinth could have been played as a land drop, imprinting World Breaker or Ugin (both colorless with MV 7+) to immediately produce {C}{C}. This would have allowed playing the land AND still having mana to cast Talisman of Impulse (using Labyrinth's {C}{C} to pay the {2} cost), ending with significantly more mana on board. By casting Talisman first, the player used their land drop opportunity suboptimally — they can still play Ugin's Labyrinth but they've already tapped their lands for the Talisman, so they get less total mana development this turn.

Casting Desperate Ritual first generates temporary floating mana before knowing what cards Wrenn's Resolve will exile. The floating {R}{R}{R} must be spent immediately, but the player hasn't yet seen what options Wrenn's Resolve would provide.

Cast Glimpse the Impossible before casting Strike It Rich. With Ruby Medallion, Strike It Rich costs 0 mana and creates a Treasure token for free, which would have provided an extra mana source to help cast the exiled cards (particularly Past in Flames at {2}{R} with medallion, which could then flashback graveyard rituals for a potential combo turn).

Failed to crack Arid Mesa before casting Wrenn's Resolve. Sacrificing the fetchland first would thin the library by one card, slightly improving the quality of the two cards exiled by Wrenn's Resolve. Additionally, fetching first would have provided an untapped land for more mana availability to cast the exiled cards.

Eldrazi Spawn tokens are 0/1 creatures that deal 0 damage when attacking. Attacking with them accomplishes nothing offensively while also tapping them, which prevents them from being sacrificed for mana on the opponent's turn if needed for instant-speed plays. The tokens' primary value is as mana sources (sacrifice for {C}), not as attackers. Sending them into combat risks losing them to blocks (though opponent has no creatures here) and removes the option to use them as mana sources until they untap.

Cast Utopia Sprawl before playing their land drop (Ghost Quarter) for the turn. While the mana wasn't needed this turn, playing lands before spells is correct sequencing - it preserves maximum flexibility and information. Ghost Quarter should be played first as it's a free action.

Attacking with 0/1 Eldrazi Spawn tokens deals 0 damage and serves no purpose. These tokens are far more valuable as mana sources (sacrifice for {C} each) to help cast spells or fuel a combo turn. Attacking risks losing them to blocks for zero benefit, and even unblocked they deal 0 damage.
Casting Pyretic Ritual during the combat phase generates RRR mana that will empty at the end of combat with nothing useful to spend it on. The ritual card is consumed for no benefit.

The player has Past in Flames available as a flashback option (it's in the graveyard and appears as a choice, likely via flashback or some other mechanism). With Ruby Medallion already on the battlefield reducing red spell costs, and multiple ritual spells (Pyretic Ritual, Desperate Ritual x2) in the graveyard, plus Past in Flames itself as a choice, the player should be considering a storm/combo turn rather than casting a single Strike It Rich for a Treasure token. Additionally, the player's reasoning mentions Strike It Rich giving 'some life' which is incorrect - it creates a Treasure token, not life. More importantly, sequencing matters: if planning to cast multiple spells this turn, playing another Ruby Medallion first (cost 2, using existing mana) would reduce costs of subsequent red spells. The Arid Mesa should also be cracked before casting spells to thin the deck and potentially fix mana. Strike It Rich with one Ruby Medallion costs 0 mana, so it's free, but the player should have at minimum cracked Arid Mesa first to get another land before committing to spell sequencing.

Casting Strike It Rich for free is fine, but the reasoning ('to get some more life') suggests confusion about the card's effect. More importantly, with Ruby Medallion reducing costs, they had the mana to cast Past in Flames from graveyard (flashback {3}{R} with Mountain + 3 Spawn tokens) and potentially chain rituals from the graveyard for a big combo turn. Strike It Rich first (free) into Past in Flames would have been optimal sequencing.

Attacking with 0/1 Eldrazi Spawn tokens deals 0 damage and risks losing them to blocks, while their primary value is as mana sources (sacrifice for {C}). The opponent has no blockers that would die to them, and the tokens deal no damage. Meanwhile, Llama4 Timmy has 3 Ruby Medallions in hand and a graveyard full of instants/sorceries - those Spawn tokens could be sacrificed for colorless mana to help cast spells or fuel future plays. Attacking with them accomplishes literally nothing (0 damage) while risking losing valuable mana sources if the opponent has any combat tricks or decides to block.

Activated Ugin's Labyrinth during combat phase when the player's own reasoning concluded they should pass priority. Tapping Ugin's Labyrinth unnecessarily during combat (either for mana with nothing to spend it on, or to return the exiled card when they may already have it) wastes the land's tap for the turn and potentially loses the {C}{C} production if the exiled card was returned to hand.

Attacking with 0/1 Eldrazi Spawn tokens deals 0 damage and accomplishes nothing, while tapping them prevents using their sacrifice ability for mana during the second main phase. With 3 Ruby Medallions in hand (costing {2} each), the colorless mana from sacrificing Spawn tokens could help cast them.

With Past in Flames available via flashback in the graveyard and multiple rituals (4x Desperate Ritual, 2x Pyretic Ritual) also in the graveyard, the correct line was to cast Past in Flames first, then chain flashback rituals to generate massive mana, then cast Glimpse and other spells. Casting Glimpse first spent mana that should have gone toward the Past in Flames combo line, potentially missing a game-winning storm turn.

Attacking with 0/1 Eldrazi Spawn tokens that deal 0 damage accomplishes nothing. These tokens are more valuable as mana sources (sacrifice for {C}) to help cast the Ruby Medallions in hand or fuel future plays from the graveyard.

Discarding Ugin's Labyrinth when there's already one on the battlefield. While the second copy has limited utility since it's legendary, Talisman of Impulse is arguably more expendable since there's already one on the battlefield as well, and the Labyrinth could potentially be played if the first one is destroyed (e.g., by Ghost Quarter from opponent). However, both are reasonable discard candidates. The more concerning question is whether Sowing Mycospawn should have been kept over some other card - but with the hand containing Emrakul, Ugin planeswalker, Devourer of Destiny, Icetill Explorer, Ghost Quarter, and Sowing Mycospawn as key cards, Ugin's Labyrinth and Talisman of Impulse are the weakest. Discarding the redundant legendary land is defensible.

Qwen3L Stoic could have activated Shifting Woodland's delirium ability (4+ card types in graveyard: sorcery, land, instant, creature) to become a copy of Sowing Mycospawn (3/3) from the graveyard, then attack for 3 damage. The activation costs {2}{G}{G} which was available from their mana base. Instead they passed without attacking.

When forced to discard to hand size, Qwen3L Stoic discarded Forest instead of a duplicate or less impactful card. With Ugin, Eye of the Storms (7 mana), Emrakul (13 mana, reduced by graveyard card types), and Devourer of Destiny (7 mana) in hand, the player has powerful finishers but needs mana to cast them. However, they already have 7 lands/mana sources on the battlefield and the Forest is the least impactful card since they have adequate green sources. The real question is whether Talisman of Impulse (a duplicate already on the battlefield) would have been a better discard. Talisman is a 2-mana rock that's somewhat redundant given the existing mana base, but Forest is a land that could be played next turn. Since they can only play one land per turn and already have good mana development, this is close but discarding the duplicate Talisman would preserve the option to play Forest as a land drop while not losing much since they already have one Talisman in play.

Attacking with 0/1 Eldrazi Spawn tokens deals 0 damage each. These tokens are more valuable as mana sources (sacrifice for {C}) than as attackers dealing 0 damage. The opponent has no reason to block them, so they deal 0 damage total. Meanwhile, sacrificing them could provide mana for casting spells. However, with only Ruby Medallions and an Arid Mesa in hand, there may not be an immediate use for the colorless mana, making this a marginal decision.

When forced to discard to hand size, Qwen3L Stoic discarded Icetill Explorer instead of a redundant Talisman of Impulse. Icetill Explorer is a powerful card that enables playing lands from the graveyard (there are multiple lands in the graveyard including Ugin's Labyrinth, Verdant Catacombs, and Forest), provides an extra land drop per turn, and has landfall mill synergy. Meanwhile, there are two copies of Talisman of Impulse in hand and one already on the battlefield, making a third copy largely redundant. Discarding a duplicate Talisman would have preserved a much higher-value card.

Failed to play Arid Mesa from hand before casting Wrenn's Resolve. Playing the land first costs nothing and could provide additional mana (by cracking it for a Mountain) to chain more spells this turn. In a storm-style deck trying to combo off, having that extra mana source available before starting the spell chain is important.

With a massive graveyard containing 4 Desperate Rituals, 2 Pyretic Rituals, Manamorphose, and multiple draw spells, Llama4 Timmy could have attempted to go off with Past in Flames this turn. By playing Arid Mesa from hand, cracking it for a Mountain, they'd have 3 mana available - exactly enough for Past in Flames with Ruby Medallion's discount. The flashback rituals would chain into enormous mana generation (each Desperate/Pyretic Ritual costs {R} with medallion, generating {R}{R}{R}), then flashback draw spells to find a finisher. Instead, they cast Artist's Talent, a setup enchantment that does almost nothing immediately.

Qwen3L Stoic is discarding to hand size and chose to discard Eldrazi Temple, which is one of the best lands for their Eldrazi strategy. Eldrazi Temple produces 2 colorless mana for casting Eldrazi spells, which is critical for casting Emrakul, Devourer of Destiny, Ugin, and Sowing Mycospawn (which has devoid). Meanwhile, they have two copies of Talisman of Impulse in hand and already have one on the battlefield. A second Talisman of Impulse is far less valuable than Eldrazi Temple, since it's redundant mana acceleration that doesn't provide the double-mana bonus for Eldrazi spells.

Cast Past in Flames via flashback spending all available mana, leaving no mana to actually flash back any instants/sorceries from the graveyard. Past in Flames gets exiled for no value. Additionally declined the Artist's Talent loot trigger which could have cycled a dead Ruby Medallion.

With untapped lands available (Gemstone Caverns, Sacred Foundry, Mountain = 3 mana), Llama4 Timmy could have cast at least one Ruby Medallion (cost 2) in addition to playing their land. With 3 Ruby Medallions in hand and a graveyard loaded with rituals and Past in Flames, deploying additional cost reducers is critical for setting up a storm kill. Each additional Medallion makes a future Past in Flames turn significantly more explosive.

Discarded Sowing Mycospawn instead of a redundant Talisman of Impulse. With one Talisman already on the battlefield and decent mana production, a second Talisman is less valuable than Sowing Mycospawn, which provides land search/ramp, a 3/3 body, and potential land exile when kicked.

Qwen3L Stoic discarded Sire of Seven Deaths, a powerful 7/7 finisher with first strike, vigilance, menace, trample, reach, lifelink, and ward-pay 7 life. This is one of their best threats. Meanwhile, they have two copies of Talisman of Impulse in hand (and already have one on the battlefield), making one of them redundant. Discarding a premium threat instead of a redundant mana rock is a significant value loss.

Discarded Icetill Explorer instead of a duplicate Talisman of Impulse. They already have a Talisman of Impulse on the battlefield, making a second copy less valuable. Icetill Explorer's ability to play lands from graveyard (5+ lands in graveyard) and make additional land drops would have been more impactful for ramping into Emrakul or Ugin.

The player should play a land first (Scalding Tarn or Mountain) before casting any spells to maximize available mana. With Past in Flames in the graveyard, rituals available, and Grapeshot for a potential storm kill, proper sequencing matters enormously. Additionally, the reasoning confuses Reckless Impulse with a damage spell, suggesting a misunderstanding of the card.

During a storm combo turn with Reckless Impulse on the stack about to exile cards, declining to activate Arid Mesa means potentially having less mana available to cast whatever Reckless Impulse reveals. With the combo turn in progress, maximizing available mana is important.

Missed attacking with Shifting Woodland as a copy of Sire of Seven Deaths (7/7 first strike, menace, trample, lifelink). Delirium is clearly active with 5+ card types in graveyard. Had plenty of mana from other lands to pay {2}{G}{G} for the activation, then attack for 7 trampling damage with lifelink against an opponent with only 0/1 Eldrazi Spawn tokens. This would deal significant damage and gain 7 life.

With 5 card types in graveyard (sorcery, land, instant, creature, planeswalker), Emrakul costs 8. By playing Wooded Foothills first and fetching a land, Qwen3L Stoic could reach 8 mana to cast Emrakul, the Promised End - gaining control of the opponent's next turn and deploying a 13/13 flying trampler. This would likely win the game against a Storm deck with only 0/1 tokens on board.

Gemstone Caverns is a legendary land that only produces colorless mana (it no longer has a luck counter at this point in the game since it was played from opening hand). Exiling it removes only a colorless mana source. The opponent's Sacred Foundry would be a better target as it produces both red and white mana, which is far more important for the Storm deck's colored mana requirements. Alternatively, exiling the Mountain (untapped colored source) or Arid Mesa (fetch land for colored mana) would be more disruptive since the Storm deck desperately needs red mana to function.

Playing a basic Mountain from hand instead of Scalding Tarn. Scalding Tarn can fetch a Mountain (same immediate effect after cracking) while thinning the deck, and playing it preserves the basic Mountain in hand for future turns. The 1 life cost is negligible for a storm deck at 16 life that needs to combo soon.

Cast Pyretic Ritual before playing a land drop. The player has Mountain and Scalding Tarn in hand and should play one first to maximize available mana before attempting to chain spells. Playing a land is free and could provide additional mana that matters for a potential storm turn with Past in Flames in the graveyard.

With Pyretic Ritual on the stack providing RRR and Ruby Medallion reducing costs by {1}, Past in Flames could be cast for {2}{R} (3 mana exactly from the ritual). This would give flashback to multiple rituals (4x Desperate Ritual, 2x Pyretic Ritual), Manamorphose x2, Strike It Rich, and crucially Grapeshot in the graveyard, enabling a potentially lethal storm turn. Wish only fetches one card and doesn't advance the storm count as efficiently.

Player passed priority in their main phase without first playing a land from hand (Scalding Tarn or Sunbaked Canyon). As a Storm deck, maximizing mana sources is crucial. They had Scalding Tarn and Sunbaked Canyon available and should have played one before passing, ensuring they don't miss their land drop and have maximum mana available for potential plays.

Prismatic Ending with X=1 can only exile permanents with mana value 1 or less (since converge counts the number of colors of mana spent). Sowing Mycospawn has mana value 4 (costs {3}{G}, though it's devoid/colorless). With X=1 and likely only 1 color of mana spent (white from Sacred Foundry), Prismatic Ending can exile permanents with mV ≤ 1. Sowing Mycospawn's mana value of 4 far exceeds this, so the spell will fail to exile it. The player wasted a Wish to get Prismatic Ending from outside the game and then targeted something it cannot legally remove. Better targets at X=1 would include Talisman of Impulse (mV 2 - still too high) or Utopia Sprawl (mV 1 - valid). Utopia Sprawl is a key mana engine for the opponent and would have been a legal and impactful target.

Cast Devourer of Destiny (6/6, exiles one permanent) instead of Emrakul, the Promised End which was castable for 7 mana (13 minus 6 card types in graveyard). Emrakul is a 13/13 flying trample with protection from instants that also gives control of the opponent's next turn - devastating against a storm combo deck at 14 life. The Mindslaver effect alone could end the game by wasting the storm player's resources.

Cast Talisman of Impulse before playing Wooded Foothills. Playing the land first (and potentially cracking it) would have given more mana available after casting the Talisman, preserving more options and leaving more mana open.

Commercial District enters tapped, meaning it won't produce mana this turn. A basic Forest would enter untapped, providing immediate mana availability. The reasoning about Commercial District producing '2 or more mana' based on nonbasics is incorrect - it's a Mountain Forest dual land that taps for {R} or {G}, not a land with scaling abilities. The surveil 1 trigger is a minor upside, but entering tapped is a real cost when you're at 15 life against a storm deck that could threaten lethal. Having untapped mana available on the opponent's turn or for your own plays next turn matters.

Qwen3L Stoic had delirium active (5+ card types in graveyard) and could have activated Shifting Woodland for {2}{G}{G} to become a copy of Sire of Seven Deaths (7/7 first strike, vigilance, menace, trample, reach, lifelink) from the graveyard, creating a devastating additional attacker. Instead, they activated Ugin's Labyrinth (tapping it for mana or returning an exiled card) while their reasoning stated they wanted to pass, gaining no meaningful advantage.

Qwen3L had enough mana to cast Sire of Seven Deaths (7/7 with first strike, vigilance, menace, trample, reach, lifelink, ward-pay 7 life) with the opponent at 8 life and no creatures. Sire would threaten lethal next turn with menace+trample against an empty board, and ward-pay 7 life makes it nearly impossible for the opponent to remove at 8 life. Instead played a 2-mana rock that adds minimal value.

At 8 life, playing Sunbaked Canyon means paying 1 life every time it's tapped for mana. On a turn where the Storm player might need to tap all lands multiple times (especially with Past in Flames flashback available), this repeated life cost adds up. Scalding Tarn would cost 1 life once to fetch an untapped Mountain, providing the same color of mana without recurring life loss, and also thin the deck for better draws.

Emrakul, the Promised End costs the same 7 mana as Sire of Seven Deaths (13 minus ~6 card types in graveyard: creature, land, sorcery, instant, planeswalker, kindred). Emrakul is a 13/13 flying trample with protection from instants, and critically its cast trigger lets you control the opponent's next turn - devastating against a Storm deck at 7 life. This is game-winning compared to just a 7/7.

message: Select a Mountain or Forest card
annotation_description: Commercial District enters tapped, which means Qwen3L Stoic loses a mana this turn compared to fetching a basic Forest (which enters untapped). With Emrakul in hand costing 13 mana (reduced by card types in graveyard), getting untapped mana sources is critical for casting it as soon as possible. The reasoning that Commercial District 'can produce at least {2} when tapped' is incorrect - it's a dual land that produces one mana ({R} or {G}), same as Forest. The only upside is the surveil 1 trigger, but the downside of entering tapped is significant when trying to deploy Emrakul. A basic Forest would have entered untapped and provided mana immediately.
